title: What is the pattern in each shape sequence?
description: Five shape sequences of the book are looked at one by one: regular polygons, complete graphs, stacked squares, stacked triangles and the speed bump shapes. Each one has a count that follows a clear pattern.
teaching_notes: One idea: count one thing in each shape, then see how the count changes from shape to shape. Watch for students who describe the picture and never count.

source: Figure it Out Q1 (Math Talk), p.11
video_script.why: The child finds a count in each shape of every sequence in the book and sees how that count changes, using the method of the solved examples.
video_script.substitution: Five sequences of shapes are looked at, one count for each.
video_script.anchor: five rows of shapes, each with a count written under every shape
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, every sequence has a pattern that we can describe

final_answer.value: polygons: 3, 4, 5, 6, ... sides; complete graphs: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 lines; stacked squares: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25; stacked triangles: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25; {{NAME_2}}: 3, 3 x 4, 3 x 4 x 4, ... segments
final_answer.spoken: yes, every sequence has a pattern

names.{{NAME_2}}: shape sequence where every line segment is replaced by a speed bump

maths_rules: regular polygons: sides 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, one more each time
complete graphs K2 to K6: lines 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, gaps 2, 3, 4, 5, the triangular numbers
stacked squares: little squares 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, the square numbers
stacked triangles: little triangles 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, the square numbers
video_script.design: Five rows of shapes stand one under the other. A count is written under each shape and the change in the counts is marked, one row at a time.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; five rows of shapes: regular polygons, complete graphs, stacked squares, stacked triangles, {{NAME_2}}, with a question mark

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.rows: the five rows of shapes appear one under the other
marks.ask: a question mark appears beside the rows

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about shape sequences.
<bookmark mark='rows'/>There are five rows of shapes. They are regular polygons, complete graphs, stacked squares, stacked triangles and the {{NAME_2}}.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Can you recognise the pattern in each row?

beats.on_screen: the five rows stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: the first row of shapes with an empty number slot under each shape

marks.way: the rows move to the side and one row stays
marks.slot: an empty number slot appears under each shape in that row

beats.removed: the other four rows move away
narration: <bookmark mark='way'/>We use the same way as the example in your book.
<bookmark mark='slot'/>We count one thing in every shape, and then see how the counts change.

beats.on_screen: Given: five shape sequences: regular polygons, complete graphs, stacked squares, stacked triangles, {{NAME_2}}

marks.given: the five names are written under the word Given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the five shape sequences of your book.

beats.on_screen: To find: the pattern in each sequence
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the pattern in each of the five sequences.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: regular polygons: sides 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, one more side each time

marks.count: the sides of each polygon are counted and the counts are written under the shapes
marks.plus: arrows marked plus 1 join the counts

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step one, count the sides of the regular polygons. They are three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine and ten.
<bookmark mark='plus'/>Each shape has one more side than the one before.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: complete graphs K2 to K6: lines 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, up by 2, 3, 4, 5

marks.count: the lines of each graph are counted and the counts are written under the shapes
marks.gap: arrows marked plus 2, plus 3, plus 4 and plus 5 join the counts

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step two, count the lines in each complete graph. They are one, three, six, ten and fifteen.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>The counts go up by two, then three, then four, then five. This is the triangular numbers.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: stacked squares and stacked triangles: both 1, 4, 9, 16, 25

marks.sq: the little squares of each stack are counted: one, four, nine, sixteen and twenty five
marks.tri: the little triangles of each stack are counted and give the same counts

narration: <bookmark mark='sq'/>Step three, count the little squares in each stack. They are one, four, nine, sixteen and twenty five.
<bookmark mark='tri'/>Count the little triangles in each stack, and we get the same counts.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: {{NAME_2}}: segments 3, then 3 x 4, then 3 x 4 x 4, then 3 x 4 x 4 x 4

marks.count: the line segments of each {{NAME_2}} shape are counted
marks.times: each count is the one before times four

narration: <bookmark mark='count'/>Step four, count the line segments in each {{NAME_2}} shape. The first has three.
<bookmark mark='times'/>The next has three times four, and the one after has three times four times four. Each time we multiply by four again.

beats.on_screen: Step 5: check a pattern: complete graph K6 has 10 + 5 = 15 lines

marks.check: the fifth count, ten, is joined to five more lines, making fifteen, which matches the lines of the last graph

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>Step five, check one pattern against its picture. The count before is ten, and five more makes fifteen, which matches the lines of the last graph.

beats.on_screen: Answer: yes; polygons gain 1 side; graphs give the triangular numbers; both stacks give the square numbers; the {{NAME_2}} multiplies by 4

marks.ans: the five patterns are boxed one under the other
marks.more: the patterns of the polygons and the graphs are lit
marks.last: the patterns of the two stacks and the last sequence are lit

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Yes, every sequence has a pattern that we can describe. <bookmark mark='more'/>Polygons gain one side each time, and graphs give the triangular numbers. <bookmark mark='last'/>Both stacks give the square numbers, and the {{NAME_2}} multiplies by four.
